subject: maths
title: Advanced 7 · Test 1
summary: A 15-question test on angle chasing, angles in polygons and geometric reasoning and proof, with a diagram for every angle question.
body:
This test covers all of Advanced 7 · Geometry: angle chasing, angles in polygons, and geometric reasoning and proof.

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator. Use scrap paper — copy the diagram and write each angle you find onto it.
- **Questions:** 15 multiple-choice questions — 2 Easy, 5 Medium, 5 Hard and 3 Challenge.

Every diagram is drawn to scale, but always work angles out with rules and reasons rather than by measuring. If you get a question wrong, Brainsnacc will show you which step went wrong, so you know which lesson to revisit.

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and each base angle is 52°. Find x, the size of ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: The base angles are both 52°, so x = 180 − 52 − 52 = 76°. 104° is the sum of the base angles, not the apex.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 180 − 52 uses only one base angle. Subtract BOTH base angles from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the equal angles are the two base angles at B and C. The apex angle at A is different.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 52 + 52 = 104 is the total of the base angles. x is what is left: 180 − 104.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles triangle ABC with AB equal to AC marked by ticks; both base angles are 52° and angle A is labelled x

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of the octagon shown?
questions.explanation: Angle sum = (8 − 2) × 180 = 1080°. 1440° comes from using 8 triangles instead of 6.
steps: Diagonals from one vertex split an 8-sided polygon into 8 − 2 = 6 triangles.

mistakes.A: Step 1: an 8-sided polygon splits into 8 − 2 = 6 triangles, not 8.
mistakes.C: Step 1: use n − 2 triangles, not n − 1: an octagon gives 6 triangles.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 5 triangles is for a heptagon. An octagon splits into 8 − 2 = 6 triangles.

questions.diagram_alt: An irregular eight-sided polygon (octagon) with no angles marked

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. ∠BAE = 34° and ∠DCE = 52°. Find x, the size of ∠AEC.
questions.explanation: A line through E parallel to AB splits x into two alternate angles, 34° and 52°, so x = 86°. 94° comes from wrongly subtracting from 180°.
steps: Draw a construction line through E parallel to AB and CD.
It splits x into 34° (alternate to ∠BAE) and 52° (alternate to ∠DCE).

mistakes.A: Step 3: the bend angle is the SUM of the two angles — do not subtract it from 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 3: the two parts of the bend angle add together; do not find their difference.
mistakes.D: Step 3: x is the angle inside the bend, less than 180°. 274° is the reflex angle outside.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a bent line from A to E to C between them; angle BAE is 34°, angle DCE is 52° and angle AEC is x

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 58° and side BC is extended to D with ∠ACD = 131°. Find x, the size of ∠ABC.
questions.explanation: The exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles: 131 = 58 + x, so x = 73°. 49° is ∠ACB, not ∠ABC.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 49° is ∠ACB, the angle at C. x is the angle at B.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the exterior angle is the SUM of ∠A and ∠B, so subtract: x = 131 − 58.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 107° would be the exterior angle at B. x is the interior angle at B.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A of 58°, angle B labelled x, and side BC extended to D with exterior angle ACD of 131°

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a regular decagon (10 sides). Find x, the size of one interior angle.
questions.explanation: Angle sum = 8 × 180 = 1440°, and 1440 ÷ 10 = 144°. 36° is the exterior angle, not the interior angle.
steps: A regular decagon has 10 equal angles.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 36° is the exterior angle (360 ÷ 10). The interior angle is 180 − 36.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 1440° is the total of all ten angles — divide by 10.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the angle sum uses n − 2 = 8 triangles, not 9: (10 − 2) × 180 = 1440.

questions.diagram_alt: A regular decagon with one interior angle labelled x

questions.prompt: In the diagram, AB ∥ CD. Which reason proves that x = y?
questions.explanation: x and y are in the same position at each crossing (above the line, right of the transversal), an F shape, so they are corresponding angles. They are not alternate because x is not between the lines.
steps: x and y are both above their line and on the right of the transversal — the same position at each crossing.
That is an F shape, so the reason is: corresponding angles, AB ∥ CD.

mistakes.A: Step 2: alternate angles are both BETWEEN the parallel lines in a Z. Here x is above AB and y is above CD — an F shape.
mistakes.C: Step 2: co-interior angles add to 180°; they are not the reason two angles are equal.
mistakes.D: Step 1: vertically opposite angles are at the same crossing point. x and y are at different crossings.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal; at AB the angle above the line on the right of the transversal is x, and at CD the angle above the line on the right is y

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC, as shown by the tick marks. Which pair of angles must be equal?
questions.explanation: The angle opposite AB is ∠ACB and the angle opposite AC is ∠ABC, so these base angles are equal. ∠BAC is between the equal sides and can be any size.
steps: AB = AC, so the triangle is isosceles.
The angle opposite side AB is ∠ACB, and the angle opposite side AC is ∠ABC.
Angles opposite equal sides are equal, so ∠ABC = ∠ACB.

mistakes.A: Step 2: equal angles sit OPPOSITE the equal sides. ∠BAC is between the equal sides, not opposite one.
mistakes.B: Step 2: ∠BAC is between the two equal sides, so it is not one of the equal pair.
mistakes.D: Step 1: only two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles, not equilateral.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with tick marks on sides AB and AC showing they are equal

questions.prompt: Three straight lines meet at a point. Above the horizontal line, the angles are x, 2x and 3x. Find the angle marked ?.
questions.explanation: x + 2x + 3x = 180, so x = 30, and the ? angle is vertically opposite 2x = 60°. 120° comes from adding to 360° instead of 180°.
steps: x, 2x and 3x sit on one side of the horizontal line, so x + 2x + 3x = 180 (angles on a straight line).
The ? angle is vertically opposite 2x, so it is 2 × 30 = 60° (vertically opposite).

mistakes.A: Step 2: 30° is x. The ? angle is vertically opposite 2x.
mistakes.B: Step 1: x, 2x and 3x lie on one side of a straight line, so they add to 180°, not 360°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 90° is 3x. Check which angle is directly opposite the ? angle — it is 2x.

questions.diagram_alt: Three straight lines crossing at one point; above the horizontal line the angles are x, 2x and 3x from right to left; below, the angle directly opposite 2x is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°, as shown. What is the sum of its interior angles?
questions.explanation: n = 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides, so the angle sum is (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°. 156° is one interior angle, not the sum.

mistakes.B: Step 2: use (n − 2) × 180 with n = 15, not n × 180.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 156° is ONE interior angle. The question asks for the sum of all of them.
mistakes.D: Step 2: use n − 2 = 13 triangles, not n − 1 = 14.

questions.diagram_alt: Part of a regular polygon: four vertices joined by three sides, with one side extended and the exterior angle of 24° marked

questions.prompt: ABCDE is a regular pentagon and ABP is an equilateral triangle inside it. Find x, the size of ∠AEP.
questions.explanation: ∠EAP = 108 − 60 = 48°, and AE = AB = AP so triangle AEP is isosceles: x = (180 − 48) ÷ 2 = 66°. 48° is the angle at A, not at E.
steps: Each angle of a regular pentagon = 540 ÷ 5 = 108°, and each angle of an equilateral triangle = 60°.
AE = AB = AP, so triangle AEP is isosceles: x = (180 − 48) ÷ 2 = 66°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 48° is ∠EAP, the angle at A. x is at E — use isosceles triangle AEP.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 180 − 48 = 132 is the total of the two equal angles in triangle AEP — halve it.
mistakes.D: Step 2: halving 108° does not give any angle here. First find ∠EAP = 108 − 60.

questions.diagram_alt: A regular pentagon ABCDE with an equilateral triangle ABP drawn inside on side AB; P is joined to E and angle AEP is labelled x

questions.prompt: In the diagram, p and q are alternate angles between lines AB and CD. Which pair of sizes would prove that AB ∥ CD?
questions.explanation: By the converse of the alternate-angle rule, the lines are parallel when p = q, so 75° and 75° proves it. The pairs that add to 180° would be the test for co-interior angles.
steps: p and q are between the lines, on opposite sides of the transversal: alternate angles.
If alternate angles are equal, the lines are parallel (converse of the alternate-angle rule).
Only p = 75°, q = 75° has equal angles.

mistakes.A: Step 2: adding to 180° is the test for CO-INTERIOR angles. Alternate angles must be equal.
mistakes.B: Step 2: alternate angles of parallel lines are equal, not supplementary.
mistakes.D: Step 2: p and q are alternate, so they must be equal for the lines to be parallel.

questions.diagram_alt: Lines AB and CD, without parallel marks, cut by a transversal; at AB the angle below the line on the right of the transversal is p, and at CD the angle above the line on the left is q

questions.prompt: AB ∥ DC and BD = BC. ∠ABD = 48°. Find x, the size of ∠DBC.
questions.explanation: ∠BDC = 48° (alternate), ∠BCD = 48° (isosceles, BD = BC), so x = 180 − 96 = 84°. 66° wrongly treats 48° as the apex angle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 48° is ∠BDC (alternate to ∠ABD). x is the angle at B inside the triangle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the 48° angles are the BASE angles of triangle BDC, not the apex. x = 180 − 2 × 48.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines with A and B on the top line and D and C on the bottom line; triangle BDC has BD equal to BC (ticks); angle ABD is 48° and angle DBC is x

questions.prompt: In a regular polygon, each interior angle i is 140° more than each exterior angle e. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: i + e = 180 and i − e = 140, so 2e = 40, e = 20° and n = 360 ÷ 20 = 18. 9 comes from taking e = 40° instead of halving.
steps: i + e = 180 (straight line) and i − e = 140 (given).

mistakes.B: Step 2: 20° is the exterior angle e. The number of sides is 360 ÷ 20.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 180 − 140 = 40 is 2e, not e. Subtracting i − e = 140 from i + e = 180 leaves 2e = 40, so halve it.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 160° is the interior angle i. Use the exterior angle to count sides.

questions.diagram_alt: Part of a regular polygon with one side extended; the interior angle is labelled i and the exterior angle is labelled e

questions.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram (AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC). Which argument proves that ∠A = ∠C?

options.A: ∠A = ∠C because they are vertically opposite angles
options.B: ∠A + ∠B = 180° (co-interior, AD ∥ BC) and ∠B + ∠C = 180° (co-interior, AB ∥ DC), so ∠A = ∠C
options.C: ∠A = ∠C because they are alternate angles, AB ∥ DC

questions.explanation: Both ∠A and ∠C equal 180° − ∠B, using two different pairs of co-interior angles. ∠A and ∠C are opposite corners, not alternate or vertically opposite angles.

mistakes.A: Step 1: vertically opposite angles are at ONE crossing point. ∠A and ∠C are at different corners.
mistakes.C: Step 1: alternate angles lie on a transversal between two parallel lines. ∠A and ∠C are not on the same transversal.
mistakes.D: Step 2: adding to 180° does not make two angles equal, and ∠A and ∠C are not co-interior.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallelogram ABCD with arrows showing AB parallel to DC and AD parallel to BC; the angles at A, B and C are marked

questions.prompt: Two mirrors meet at 70°. A light beam hits mirror 1 and bounces off at 30° to it, as shown, then hits mirror 2. Find x, the angle between the beam and mirror 2.
questions.explanation: The beam and the two mirrors make a triangle with angles 70°, 30° and x, so x = 180 − 70 − 30 = 80°. 40° (70 − 30) uses no rule.
steps: The reflected beam, mirror 1 and mirror 2 form a triangle.
Its angles are 70° (between the mirrors), 30° (beam and mirror 1) and x.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 70 − 30 uses no angle rule. The beam and the two mirrors form a triangle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the beam does not meet mirror 2 at the same angle as mirror 1. Use the triangle formed by the beam and the mirrors.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 100° is the sum of the two known angles. x is what is left of 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: Two mirrors meeting at a point with an angle of 70° between them; a beam reflects off mirror 1, making 30° with it on both sides, and travels to mirror 2, where the angle between the beam and mirror 2 is x
